text: Ivan's point landed hardest. A retracted paper grounding an answer would generate a royalty event in our own scheme. Retraction status has to live in the telemetry, checked against Retraction Watch, which is one more reason the labs should fund it. Leslie's legibility warning is real. If DOIs become the price of payment, we've rebuilt the toll booth. Adrian is right that the meter defines the right, and that sharpens my case for an open protocol with many witnesses. I'll concede Nick's point: per-answer payment works for retrieval, but training may need coarser payouts. Adam's worry about lab money stung. Later I want to argue that labs should pay for infrastructure as disclosed obligations, not patronage. It needs a prospectus.

Brent's grand bargain framing mattered most. It's my circulatory-economy argument, said by someone inside Microsoft, which makes it harder to wave off. Alex's robots.txt audit sharpened it. If publishers block the training bot and leave the grounding bot alone, then consent signals are already failing, and that argues for separate controls carried in the protocol. Nick's quasi-enclosure is uncomfortable because it's accurate: subsidized club goods can be withdrawn. Kara's apprenticeship point I dismissed too quickly as mentorship design. Mentorship design still costs money, and nobody is paying for it. Nick and Brent got me on openness too. Open with no payback just feeds the nearest mill. Later I want to argue that walls fail and consent-only fails, and that what should replace both is telemetry, disclosed obligations, and payment that follows use.

Adrian's history mattered most. UL grew out of the fire insurers and ended up policing authenticity for Apple and Disney with no public oversight. Chokepoints get repurposed. My "many witnesses" answer holds, but only if the witnesses aren't all paid by one side. Alex's point sharpened that: the measurement currency can't be set by whoever takes a cut. Ivan's numbers keep biting too. Telemetry carrying correction status only carries corrections that happened, so funding sleuths belongs on the lab ledger. Nick's commons-rent tax is closer to my prospectus than I expected. Opacity becomes a line item. Later I want to argue for disclosure in both places, securities filings and citation logs, as one regime. Kara still deserves a named payer for apprenticeship.

James and Henry landed hardest. A retrieval meter pays the lamp post twice, and I'd written that myself twenty years ago about long-tail aggregators. So I split the jobs: per-use royalties for retrieval, disclosed obligations for null results and infrastructure. Tamar's daycare fee unsettled me more. "Whatever gets measured can get paid" might crowd out the norms that make editors and sleuths work. Brent's firm-level charge is the likely way out, but it should be tested first. Mike's audit is the gap in my own scheme. A cited event can be post-hoc decoration and still earn a royalty. Adrian's rotating wardens answer who guards the guards better than "many witnesses" alone. Later I want to push for paying for audits as well as retrieval.

Pomerantsev landed hardest. Pravda-style networks are built to be retrieved, so a per-grounding royalty pays the flooders most. Ivan and Steven made the same point from the volume side. My split still holds, but per-use payment now needs a coordination flag and support audits before anything pays out. Banaji is right that self-reported grounding by the payer is a conflict, which makes Alex's two-witness design essential rather than nice to have. Turkle and Caulfield sharpened something I'd underplayed. A citation that dead-ends at a paywall, or that nobody clicks, isn't circulation. Later I want to add click-through to the telemetry and make an openable passage a licence condition. Kara asked who carries this. I should volunteer for the disclosure piece.

Geoffrey corrected me fairly. Crossref tells you a paper exists and who registered it, not whether it's true. I lumped legitimacy in with quality, and the standard I'm drafting can't make that mistake. Ivan's "blank reads as clean" goes into the spec: "not checked" has to be its own value, separate from "no correction found." Chan worries me most. My disclosure standard, taken together with ORCID and manifests, could become exactly the compliance toll he described, drafted from rooms like this one. It needs governance that includes SciELO and Redalyc from the start. Krakauer's warning fits my own scheme too, since payment that follows use can end up scoring checkers by volume. I committed only to the drafting. Later I want to push hard, by name, for someone to fund the apprentices.

Adam's "grateful but not reassured" landed hardest. Naming the labs as payer for apprentices answers Kara, but money given directly buys loyalty. The lab obligation has to flow into a pool held by neutral infrastructure, with several payers and published flows, as Ivan designed for sleuths. Otherwise it's patronage with a prospectus stapled on. Leslie caught me too. I said "governed with SciELO and Redalyc from the start," but I'm drafting the standard in Cambridge. Co-drafting means they hold the pen on the first version, and I should ask them this week, not after. Esther's sunset clause belongs in my standard. Later I want to merge my disclosure regime with Nick's tax: disclosed receipts are what lower the rent.

Alex landed hardest. He said the measurement currency can't be set by anyone who takes a margin on the count, including himself. That applies to O'Reilly Answers too. We compute our own royalties, so my own product needs an outside auditor before I can offer it as proof. Nick's "organize before metering" stings. Disclosed obligations without organized producers are still patronage with a prospectus. Amy's consolidation warning is my enshittification argument turned on me: deals cluster among the biggest players. I'll take her renegotiation terms and her pilots with published costs. On who reads the logs, I still say anyone, but raw traces might need a delay. Geoffrey's mirrors outside the US belong in the standard. Later, I'll commit publicly to co-drafting with SciELO and Redalyc, starting this week.
